claim: Ebola is a deadly virus that causes frequent disease outbreaks in the human population.
source: Ebola is a deadly virus that causes frequent disease outbreaks in the human population.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the subsequent analysis of outbreak rates and case fatality ratios presented in the manuscript.

claim: The effective reproductive ratio of Ebola is just less than 1.
source: The results show a fast rate of new outbreaks, a high case fatality ratio, and an effective reproductive ratio of just less than 1.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the statistical analysis presented in Figures 2 and 4, showing Rt estimates of 0.88[0.64,0.96] and 0.94[0.87,0.99].

claim: Ebola virus disease is an often fatal disease of humans that is not vaccine-preventable and has no specific treatment.
source: Ebola virus disease is an often fatal disease of humans that is not vaccine-preventable and has no specific treatment.
evidence: This statement draws on established medical knowledge about Ebola as of the time of writing.

claim: A total of 25 outbreaks of Ebola have occurred since the first observed cases in humans in 1976.
source: A total of 25 outbreaks, believed to have arisen due to zoonotic transmission from wild mammals, have occurred since the first observed cases in humans in 1976 (World Health Organisation, 2014a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to WHO data.

claim: Ebola outbreaks are believed to have arisen due to zoonotic transmission from wild mammals.
source: A total of 25 outbreaks, believed to have arisen due to zoonotic transmission from wild mammals, have occurred since the first observed cases in humans in 1976 (World Health Organisation, 2014a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to WHO data and represents the scientific understanding of Ebola transmission origins.

claim: The current epidemic is the largest Ebola outbreak to date.
source: The current epidemic is the largest to date (World Health Organisation, 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to WHO data from 2014.

claim: Similar R₀ estimates to those from 1995 and 2000 outbreaks were obtained for the ongoing outbreak.
source: with similar results obtained for the ongoing outbreak (Althaus, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a 2014 study.

claim: The mean time between Ebola outbreaks is 1.49[1.02,2.24] years.
source: Figure 1A showing the empirical distribution of times between outbreaks together with the fitted model distribution that has mean 1.49[1.02,2.24] years between outbreaks
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the statistical analysis of outbreak timing data shown in Figure 1A and 1C.

claim: The effective reproductive ratio Rt for completed outbreaks is estimated to be 0.88[0.64,0.96].
source: Figure 2C showing the posterior for the reproductive ratio, which is estimated to be Rt=0.88[0.64,0.96].
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the Bayesian statistical analysis of completed outbreak data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The geometric parameter p for completed outbreaks is estimated to be 0.089[0.029,0.19].
source: Figure 2D shows the posterior for the geometric parameter, which is estimated to be p=0.089[0.029,0.19].
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the Bayesian statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Ebola outbreaks show behaviour that is typical of near-critical branching processes, which often become extinct early but also often grow to significant size before extinction.
source: Figure 3A shows a set of 24 outbreaks simulated from a continuous-time Markov chain with the same probability distribution for final size as the estimated model. These show behaviour that is typical of near-critical branching processes, which often becoming extinct early but also often grows to significant size before extinction.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3A and represents an inference about the nature of Ebola outbreak dynamics.

claim: The parameters of the Ebola transmission model are identifiable from outbreak final size data.
source: Figure 3B plots the likelihood surface for these simulated data showing parameter identifiability.
evidence: This claim is supported by the likelihood contour analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: When completed outbreak data are augmented by an outbreak of size 1000-5000, the probability of such an additional outbreak is estimated to be 0.023[0.0015,0.088].
source: Figure 4B shows the posterior for the probability of the additional outbreak, which is estimated to be 0.023[0.0015,0.088].
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the Bayesian statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: When completed outbreak data are augmented by an outbreak of size 1000-5000, the effective reproductive ratio Rt is estimated to be 0.94[0.87,0.99].
source: Figure 4C shows the posterior for the reproductive ratio, which is estimated to be Rt=0.94[0.87,0.99]
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the Bayesian statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When completed outbreak data are augmented by an outbreak of size 1000-5000, the geometric parameter p is estimated to be 0.11[0.054,0.21].
source: Figure 4D shows the posterior for the geometric parameter, which is estimated to be p=0.11[0.054,0.21].
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the Bayesian statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The rate of new Ebola epidemics is high.
source: The results obtained point to the following conclusions about Ebola transmission dynamics. (i) The rate of new epidemics and CFR are both high, but with significant variability from outbreak to outbreak.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the analysis showing mean time between outbreaks of 1.49 years.

claim: The case fatality ratio (CFR) of Ebola is high.
source: The results obtained point to the following conclusions about Ebola transmission dynamics. (i) The rate of new epidemics and CFR are both high, but with significant variability from outbreak to outbreak.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the CFR analysis shown in Figure 1B with beta distribution parameters α=6.1[2.8,11] and β=3.1[1.5,5.9].

claim: There is significant variability in Ebola case fatality ratio from outbreak to outbreak.
source: The results obtained point to the following conclusions about Ebola transmission dynamics. (i) The rate of new epidemics and CFR are both high, but with significant variability from outbreak to outbreak.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the beta distribution fit to CFR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: It is possible that a number of small Ebola outbreaks were not recorded by the WHO.
source: Also, it is possible that a number of small outbreaks were not recorded by the WHO.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential data limitations.

claim: Unrecorded small outbreaks could be addressed through incorporation of additional variability into the model through introduction of explicit overdispersal parameters.
source: This could be addressed through incorporation of additional variability into the model through introduction of explicit overdispersal parameters as in the study by Lloyd-Smith et al. (Lloyd-Smith et al., 2005) and Blumberg and Lloyd-Smith (Blumberg and Lloyd-Smith, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous methodological studies and represents a suggestion for future work.

claim: For the data currently available there was no strong evidence for overdispersal beyond that implied by the geometric distributions.
source: although for the data currently available there was no strong evidence for overdispersal beyond that implied by the geometric distributions.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis performed in the study.

claim: The results give support to appeals for greater resources to respond to the ongoing epidemic.
source: All of these conclusions suggest no reason for complacency and give support to appeals for greater resources to respond to the ongoing epidemic (Médecins Sans Frontières, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the results with citation to an appeal for resources.

claim: The analysis is based on time between outbreaks, number of deaths, and final number of cases for all 24 completed Ebola outbreaks reported by the WHO.
source: In this study, a different approach is taken based on using the time between outbreaks, number of deaths, and final number of cases, for all 24 completed Ebola outbreaks reported by the World Health Organisation (World Health Organisation, 2014a).
evidence: This describes the data sources used in the study.

claim: The start of new Ebola outbreaks is modeled as a memoryless Poisson process with a rate λ.
source: First, we model the start of new outbreaks as a 'memoryless' Poisson process with a rate λ.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach taken in the study.

claim: Each new Ebola outbreak has a case fatality ratio picked from a beta distribution.
source: Secondly, we assume that each new outbreak has a case fatality ratio (CFR—the probability that a case will die) picked from a beta distribution.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach taken in the study.

claim: Bayesian MCMC with uninformative priors was used to fit all models.
source: Bayesian MCMC with uninformative priors was used to fit all models (Gilks et al., 1995).
evidence: This describes the statistical methodology with citation.

claim: Doubts have been raised in the literature about the use of final size data for emerging diseases.
source: Since doubts have been raised in the literature about the use of final size data for emerging diseases (Drake, 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A simulation study was performed to test identifiability of parameters from final size data.
source: a simulation study was also performed to test identifiability, although a recent study by Blumberg and Lloyd-Smith (Blumberg and Lloyd-Smith, 2013) of joint identifiability of two parameters in a related model is also highly relevant in this context.
evidence: This describes a methodological component of the study with citation to related work.

claim: Multimodality was not observed in the parameter spaces.
source: The parameter spaces involved are low-dimensional enough that large-scale sweeps can be performed to check for multimodality, which was not observed
evidence: This is a finding from the computational analysis.

claim: Convergence of the MCMC chains was observed to be fast and independent of initial conditions.
source: and convergence of the chains was observed to be fast and independent of initial conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational analysis.

claim: The real-time incidence curves in the simulation study are produced by modelling the geometric distributions as arising from Poissonian transmission with exponentially distributed rates.
source: For the simulation study, the real-time incidence curves are produced by modelling the geometric distributions as arising from Poissonian transmission with exponentially distributed rates.
evidence: This describes the simulation methodology.

claim: MATLAB code to reproduce the analysis is available at https://github.com/thomasallanhouse/elife-ebola-code.
source: MATLAB code to reproduce the analysis of this paper is available at: https://github.com/thomasallanhouse/elife-ebola-code.
evidence: This is a statement about data/code availability.

claim: The start of new outbreaks in the human population is modeled as a Poisson process of rate λ.
source: We model the start of new outbreaks in the human population as a Poisson process of rate λ.
evidence: This is a mathematical model specification.
